current.note: Notebooks cover nearly every authoring need in Fabric data engineering: PySpark, Scala, SQL, and pure Python in one place, with built-in resources, Git integration, and tight links to lakehouses and pipelines. Day-to-day use is less polished, since session start-up can be slow, errors in long Spark runs are hard to trace, and the editing experience still feels uneven next to dedicated IDEs. Capacity use is reasonable when sessions are sized and shut down with care, and the item shows steady investment with new capabilities arriving regularly.

current.note: Environment is the right place to pin a Spark runtime, Spark compute settings, and shared libraries once and attach them to many notebooks and Spark job definitions. That keeps per-notebook install cells out of the code and avoids paying for repeated setup in every session. Publishing changes is slow, though, and failed library installs are hard to diagnose. Sessions that use custom libraries also start more slowly than the default pools.

current.note: Pipeline is the orchestration backbone of Fabric data engineering, with a full set of activities for moving data, running notebooks and Spark jobs, and chaining them together with branching, looping, and scheduling. Authoring is mostly clear and the canvas holds up well as workflows grow, though debugging a failed run in a deeply nested pipeline can still mean digging through several layers of activity output. Capacity use is reasonable for light orchestration but climbs on copy-heavy workloads, where data movement consumes more than a purpose-built alternative would. Microsoft keeps investing in it as the center of the workload, so it is a safe choice to build on.

current.note: Dataflow Gen2 is the easiest way in Fabric to get from a messy source to a clean table: the Power Query editor is visual and forgiving, previews are immediate, and a failed refresh is usually simple to trace to the step that caused it. That polish hides real limits, because the item handles only a narrow range of scenarios well and teams hit walls on large volumes

current.note: The Lakehouse is the natural home for data in Fabric: Delta tables and raw files sit side by side in OneLake, with a SQL analytics endpoint, shortcuts, and schema support, and Spark, SQL, and Power BI can all work on the same copy. It covers essentially every storage scenario we would ask of it, and it is cheap to run for the result you get. What holds it back is day-to-day polish, since table maintenance such as compaction and vacuuming still needs deliberate attention and troubleshooting a slow or stale SQL endpoint is less obvious than it should be. As a first review there is no earlier direction to report, but investment across the platform is clearly heavy and the Lakehouse is at the center of it.

current.note: Fabric Warehouse is a fully transactional T-SQL engine over open Delta storage, and it handles multi-table transactions, cross-database queries, and zero-copy cloning well enough to be the natural home for governed, SQL-first analytics. Authoring, monitoring, and troubleshooting are smooth, and the roadmap shows steady investment in closing the remaining T-SQL surface gaps. Those gaps still matter, since some familiar constructs and migration paths from traditional SQL Server remain unsupported, and heavy or poorly tuned workloads can consume more capacity than comparable Lakehouse queries would. This is the first review, so there is no prior direction to report.

current.note: SQL database in Fabric brings a familiar, autonomous SQL Server-engine experience into the platform, with automatic mirroring to OneLake that makes transactional data available for analytics without any pipeline work. Setup is quick and the tooling will feel natural to anyone who already knows T-SQL, though the feature set still has gaps compared with a full Azure SQL deployment. Capacity consumption is the main drawback, since the database draws on CUs even when activity is light, which makes it a pricier way to host small or intermittent workloads. Microsoft is clearly investing in it as the operational counterpart to the lakehouse and warehouse, so the trajectory looks strong.

It is read-only, so you can't write back through it. Strong momentum suggests it will keep getting better.

current.note: Semantic models are the governed center of Power BI: DAX measures, row-level security, calculation groups, Direct Lake, and composite models cover nearly every analytical scenario, and Git integration and XMLA endpoints let teams manage them like real engineering assets. Refresh and storage costs are reasonable for most workloads, especially when Direct Lake avoids duplicating data into the model. Day-to-day authoring and troubleshooting are less smooth, since diagnosing slow DAX, refresh failures, or fallback to DirectQuery often means leaving the main interface for external tools. Microsoft's continued investment in the model as the shared layer for reports, Copilot, and notebooks keeps its direction clearly positive.

current.note: Ontology gives Fabric a shared business vocabulary, with entity types, relationships, and properties mapped onto OneLake data, so that agents and downstream tools can reason over the same definitions. The idea is sound, but the preview still has gaps in modeling and binding that stop it from covering many everyday scenarios. Setup is also hard to follow, and errors give little help in finding the cause.

current.note: OneLake catalog gives you one place to discover, govern, and understand data across every workspace, with endorsement, lineage, and security insight sitting right beside the items they describe. It is quick to learn and easy to trust, and it covers the full job of finding and managing data without needing add-on tooling. The one drag is capacity: browsing and governance activity at scale uses more compute than its lightweight feel would suggest. Since this is the first review, there is no earlier direction to compare against, but Microsoft's steady investment suggests it will keep deepening.

current.note: Shortcuts let you reference data in place across OneLake, ADLS, S3, and other sources without copying it, and they cover nearly every scenario that matters, including table and file sources, cross-workspace sharing, and transparent use from Spark, SQL, and Power BI. Because nothing is duplicated, there is little pipeline or storage overhead, and capacity cost stays low for most reads. Where it falls short is day-to-day handling: creating shortcuts takes more clicks than it should, and when one breaks from an expired credential, a moved target, or a permissions mismatch, the error messages rarely say which it was. Momentum is strong, with steady new source types and wider support across workloads, though this is a first review with no earlier direction to compare against.
